actors.role: His capability approach underpins the Human Development Index, providing a theoretical foundation for measuring wellbeing beyond monetary output.

significance.justification: Sen’s capability approach provides a philosophical basis for re‑thinking welfare measurement.
significance.supporting_text: The capability approach… critiques welfare economics… Sen was convinced by the UN representatives to go ahead with a simplified version.

actors.name: King of Bhutan
actors.description: Monarch of Bhutan who launched the Gross National Happiness programme in the early 1970s.
actors.role: Initiated one of the earliest and most cited Beyond‑GDP initiatives, providing a national framework that values wellbeing and nature over GDP.
actors.supporting_text: One of the earliest and most cited Beyond-GDP initiatives is the programme on Gross National Happiness which was initiated by the King of Bhutan in the early 1970s.

significance.justification: His initiation of Gross National Happiness introduced an alternative to GDP, showing a new pathway for valuing nature.
significance.supporting_text: One of the earliest and most cited Beyond‑GDP initiatives is the programme on Gross National Happiness which was initiated by the King of Bhutan in the early 1970s.

actors.name: Commission for Sustainable Development (CSD)
actors.description: A United Nations body that, in 1995, proposed a set of Sustainable Development Indicators.
actors.role: Proposed a benchmark indicator set for measuring progress beyond GDP, based on stakeholder deliberations among UN member states.
actors.supporting_text: In 1995 the Commission for Sustainable Development (CSD) proposed such an indicator set. The CSD indicators were based on stakeholder deliberations between the various countries of the UN.

significance.justification: CSD proposed a benchmark indicator set and mobilised stakeholder deliberations, advancing collective measurement efforts.
significance.supporting_text: In 1995 the Commission for Sustainable Development (CSD) proposed such an indicator set. They were a major boost to the measurement of Beyond‑GDP.

actors.name: Eurostat
actors.description: Statistical office of the European Union that produces European-wide statistical reports.
actors.role: Produced the European Sustainable Development Indicator set and the Well‑being Report, providing alternative metrics to GDP for EU member states.
actors.supporting_text: All EU28 countries created their own indicator set, and there was also a European SDI which was produced by Eurostat. Indicator sets also became popular for other topics outside of sustainable development. For example, Eurostat's Well-being Report has a range of indicators...

significance.justification: Eurostat produced European SDI and Well‑being Report, raising visibility of alternative wellbeing metrics.
significance.supporting_text: Eurostat’s Well‑being Report has a range of indicators and the European SDI which was produced by Eurostat.

actors.name: United Nations Economic Commission for Europe (UNECE)
actors.description: UN regional commission that works on economic integration and sustainable development in Europe.
actors.role: Co‑created the Working Group for Statistics on Sustainable Development and later the Task Force on Measuring Sustainable Development, shaping conceptual indicator frameworks.
actors.supporting_text: In 2004, the UNECE, OECD and Eurostat (European Commission) created the Working Group for Statistics on Sustainable Development (WGSSD)... In 2009, just after the publication of the Stiglitz Report, the joint UNECE/OECD/Eurostat Task Force on Measuring Sustainable Development (TFSD) was created.

significance.justification: UNECE helped establish WGSSD and TFSD, providing institutional frameworks for sustainable‑development statistics.
significance.supporting_text: In 2004, the UNECE, OECD and Eurostat ... created the Working Group for Statistics on Sustainable Development (WGSSD).

actors.name: Working Group for Statistics on Sustainable Development (WGSSD)
actors.description: A joint task‑force of UNECE, OECD and Eurostat established to develop sustainable‑development statistics.
actors.role: Produced a report that influenced the Stiglitz Report and laid groundwork for conceptual (Type 4) indicator sets.
actors.supporting_text: In 2004, the UNECE, OECD and Eurostat (European Commission) created the Working Group for Statistics on Sustainable Development (WGSSD). The group built on the idea of wealth accounting...

significance.justification: WGSSD’s report introduced wealth‑accounting concepts that shaped later conceptual indicator frameworks.
significance.supporting_text: The group built on the idea of wealth accounting... WGSSD Report ... had a significant influence on the Stiglitz Report.

actors.name: Task Force on Measuring Sustainable Development (TFSD)
actors.description: Successor to the WGSSD, a joint UNECE/OECD/Eurostat task‑force created in 2009.
actors.role: Developed a set of Type 4 (conceptual) indicators and built on the Stiglitz Report’s framework.
actors.supporting_text: In 2009, just after the publication of the Stiglitz Report, the joint UNECE/OECD/Eurostat Task Force on Measuring Sustainable Development (TFSD) was created. The TFSD built on the conceptual framework of the Stiglitz Report...

significance.justification: TFSD continued the conceptual approach of the Stiglitz Report, creating Type 4 indicators.
significance.supporting_text: The TFSD built on the conceptual framework of the Stiglitz Report and also created a set of (Type 4) indicators.

actors.name: EU28 countries
actors.description: The 28 member states of the European Union (as of the time of writing).
actors.role: Each created its own Sustainable Development Indicator dashboard, illustrating national adoption of Beyond‑GDP metrics.
actors.supporting_text: All EU28 countries created their own indicator set, and there was also a European SDI which was produced by Eurostat.

significance.justification: All EU28 nations developed their own SDI dashboards, demonstrating coordinated national action.
significance.supporting_text: All EU28 countries created their own indicator set, and there was also a European SDI which was produced by Eurostat.

actors.name: Statistical Commission of the United Nations
actors.description: The highest‑level statistical body of the United Nations that oversees the development of global statistical standards.
actors.role: Adopted the System of Environmental Economic Accounting 2012 – Central Framework, formalising the SEEA as an official statistical standard.
actors.supporting_text: After a lengthy deliberation process the System of Environmental Economic Accounting 2012 - Central Framework was adopted by the Statistical Commission of the United Nations.

significance.justification: Adopted the 2012 SEEA framework, institutionalising the standard.
significance.supporting_text: … was adopted by the Statistical Commission of the United Nations.

actors.name: UN Statistical Division
actors.description: A division of the United Nations Statistics Division that coordinates global statistical activities and standards.
actors.role: Set an explicit target for a hundred countries to start producing SEEA accounts by 2020, promoting widespread implementation.
actors.supporting_text: The UN Statistical Division has made it its explicit aim to have a hundred countries start producing SEEA account by 2020.

significance.justification: Sets a target for widespread production of SEEA accounts, encouraging global uptake.
significance.supporting_text: The UN Statistical Division has made it its explicit aim to have a hundred countries start producing SEEA account by 2020.

actors.name: Six major international institutes
actors.description: A group of six leading international statistical and economic institutes that collaborated on the SEEA.
actors.role: Co‑authored and prepared the SEEA 2003 edition under their auspices, providing essential institutional backing.
actors.supporting_text: The SEEA was prepared under the auspices of the six major international institutes.

significance.justification: Co‑authored and prepared the SEEA, demonstrating coordinated institutional effort.
significance.supporting_text: The SEEA was prepared under the auspices of the six major international institutes.

actors.name: Statistical offices of the UN member states
actors.description: National statistical agencies of United Nations member countries.
actors.role: Agreed to the SEEA handbook, contributing to its institutional legitimacy and global uptake.
actors.supporting_text: Getting this handbook agreed by six international institutes and all the statistical offices of the UN member states is a major achievement.

significance.justification: Their agreement was essential for the SEEA’s institutional legitimacy.
significance.supporting_text: Getting this handbook agreed by six international institutes and all the statistical offices of the UN member states is a major achievement.

actors.name: U.S. Congress
actors.description: The legislative body of the United States that discontinued the country’s environmental accounts in the 1990s.
actors.role: By ending the environmental accounts program, it created a major institutional barrier to the adoption of Beyond‑GDP indicators in the United States.
actors.supporting_text: The environmental accounts of the United States were discontinued in the 1990s by the US Congress.

significance.justification: Discontinued US environmental accounts, directly blocking progress toward alternative metrics.
significance.supporting_text: The environmental accounts of the United States were discontinued in the 1990s by the US Congress.

actors.name: Bleys and Whitby
actors.description: Scholars who authored a 2015 assessment of Beyond‑GDP initiatives.
actors.role: Provided a comprehensive analysis of the requirements (timeliness, robustness, communication, standardised methodology) for successful adoption of alternative wellbeing and sustainability indicators.
actors.supporting_text: Bleys and Whitby (2015) probably provide the most comprehensive assessment in this direction. It names timeliness, robustness and communication as well as a standardised methodology as important requirements for success.

significance.justification: Their comprehensive assessment identifies key requirements that could shift the system toward effective Beyond‑GDP adoption.
significance.supporting_text: Bleys and Whitby (2015) probably provide the most comprehensive assessment… It names timeliness, robustness and communication… as important requirements for success.

actors.name: Hayden and Wilson
actors.description: Researchers who examined the uptake of Beyond‑GDP indicators in Canada in a 2016 study.
actors.role: Investigated why the adoption of alternative indicators has been disappointing in Canada and concluded that merely producing an indicator does not automatically change society.
actors.supporting_text: Hayden and Wilson (2016) investigate the "disappointing" uptake of Beyond‑GDP indicators in Canada. They conclude euphemistically that the idea that simply producing an indicator will suddenly change society "is certainly not borne out by the Canadian experience to date".

significance.justification: Their study highlights the disappointing uptake of Beyond‑GDP indicators, exposing a barrier to progress.
significance.supporting_text: Hayden and Wilson (2016) investigate the “disappointing” uptake of Beyond‑GDP indicators in Canada.

actors.name: Costanza et al.
actors.description: A research team led by Robert Costanza that published a 2017 paper linking society’s focus on GDP to addiction theory.
actors.role: Introduced the analogy of GDP addiction and suggested that motivational‑interviewing techniques could be adapted to shift societal values toward wellbeing and sustainability.
actors.supporting_text: In a novel paper, Costanza et al. (2017) liken society's focus on economic growth to a real addiction. They explore how methods that are used for addicts might be adopted at the societal level. For example, Motivational Interviewing (MI) is based on engaging addicts in a positive discussion of their goals, motives and futures.

significance.justification: They propose a novel addiction‑framework and MI approach, suggesting a non‑linear shift in societal attitudes toward GDP.
significance.supporting_text: Costanza et al. (2017) liken society’s focus on economic growth to a real addiction… explore how methods used for addicts might be adopted.
